strengths: The paper targets an ambitious and practically important objective: building a universal model for tabular outlier detection (OD) that can generalize across heterogeneous datasets with different feature dimensions without retraining.

The experimental section evaluates on 15 real-world benchmark datasets from ADBench and compares against a wide array of 15 baselines spanning both classic unsupervised methods and recent deep learning approaches.

The ablation studies systematically examine several design choices, including the number of historical training datasets, the number of Gaussian kernel bandwidths, subsampling data augmentation, and the architectural components (GNN/GT vs. MLP).
weaknesses: Unfair supervision compared to baselines: The paper compares UniOD directly against purely unsupervised OD methods (e.g., Isolation Forest, ECOD, LOF, DSVDD, NeutralAD). However, UniOD is trained on 15 external datasets with complete ground-truth binary outlier labels. Gaining supervision from historical datasets alters the problem formulation, yet the paper does not compare against meta-learning or transfer learning baselines properly tailored for supervised transfer.

Marginal empirical gain over simple, unsupervised baselines: Despite having access to historical supervision and employing a complex GIN + Graph Transformer architecture, UniOD achieves an average AUROC of 78.9% compared to 76.6% for standard unsupervised Isolation Forest (IF), and in terms of AUPRC, Isolation Forest actually outperforms UniOD (45.89% vs. 45.43%). Given the significant computational overhead and supervision requirement, the performance benefits are unconvincing.

Scalability and computational feasibility issues: The method computes full pairwise Gaussian kernel matrices and their truncated SVD, followed by all-to-all attention in a Graph Transformer ($O(N^2)$ complexity). Several benchmark datasets in Table 6 contain hundreds of thousands of samples (e.g., Cover at ~286k, CelebA at ~202k, Skin at ~245k). Storing and decomposing dense $N \times N$ matrices of this scale is computationally prohibitive, yet the paper does not explain how such large datasets were processed (e.g., Nyström approximation, mini-batching) or whether severe subsampling was applied.

Lack of technical addressing of spectral embedding issues: Using truncated SVD of the kernel matrix as node features inherits classical sign and basis ambiguity (eigenvectors are defined only up to a sign flip $\pm v$). Feeding raw SVD coordinates into standard GNNs and MLPs without sign-invariant or canonical orientation mechanisms typically causes arbitrary representation flips between training and test graphs.

Preprocessing and tabular data heterogeneity: Computing Euclidean distance across arbitrary tabular features is highly sensitive to feature scales and categorical variables. The manuscript does not discuss how disparate data types, categorical features, or varying feature scales were handled prior to Gaussian kernel evaluation.

Presentation and writing quality: The manuscript contains multiple typos and presentation oversights (e.g., duplicate entries in the references such as Breunig et al. 2000 and Livernoche et al. 2023, typos such as 'Subsapmling' in Algorithm 1, 'neueral-network-computing', 'trnasformation', and 'converting time dost' in Section F).

strengths: The paper tackles an interesting and ambitious problem: building a foundation/universal outlier detection model capable of zero-shot transfer across tabular datasets from diverse domains with varying feature dimensions.
The experimental section compares the proposed method against an extensive suite of 15 baseline algorithms on 15 benchmark datasets from ADBench.
The paper provides detailed ablation experiments regarding the number of historical datasets, bandwidth scales, and individual components (subsampling and GNN layers).
weaknesses: Unresolved Sign and Basis Ambiguity in Spectral Embeddings: In Eq. (3), node features are defined using the leading eigenvectors obtained via SVD of the adjacency matrix. Eigenvectors have inherent sign ambiguity (i.e., if $u$ is an eigenvector, so is $-u$), and standard eigensolvers return arbitrary signs. Furthermore, across two distinct graphs from entirely different domains, there is no canonical alignment or correspondence between the $j$-th eigenvector coordinates. Because standard GIN/MLP layers expect consistent channel semantics, treating arbitrary SVD coordinates as fixed input channels without sign-invariant or basis-invariant architectures (e.g., SignNet/BasisNet) is a major methodological flaw.

Unfair Comparison and Supervision Discrepancy: The paper positions UniOD within outlier detection (OD), emphasizing that OD seeks to identify outliers in unlabeled datasets. However, UniOD is trained in a supervised manner on ground-truth labels across 15 historical datasets. Almost all baselines in Table 2 (IF, kNN, LOF, ECOD, DSVDD, NeutralAD, ICL, SLAD, DTE, DPAD, ODIM) are completely unsupervised methods that do not use any labeled data. Despite using 15 labeled datasets, UniOD only marginally outperforms Isolation Forest (IF, 2008) in AUROC (78.93% vs 76.62%) and is actually outperformed by IF on AUPRC (45.43% vs 45.89%).

Scalability and Memory Feasibility Concerns: Computing a full pairwise Gaussian similarity matrix and computing its SVD scales as $O(n^2)$ space and $O(n^3)$ (or $O(n^2 d^*)$) time. Furthermore, the Graph Transformer requires $O(n^2)$ memory for full self-attention. Several historical datasets listed in Table 6 have massive sample sizes (e.g., http with 567,498 samples, cover with 286,048 samples, skin with 245,057 samples, celeba with 202,599 samples). Even after the 60% subsampling mentioned in Section 3.2.3, datasets like http contain over 340,000 nodes. Storing a dense adjacency matrix for 340,000 nodes requires hundreds of gigabytes of RAM, which cannot fit into the specified single NVIDIA A40 GPU (48 GB VRAM). The paper does not clarify how these massive graphs were processed without running out of memory.

Time Complexity Claims: The claim that UniOD has 'lower time complexity' than deep learning baselines is misleading. While inference bypasses per-dataset gradient descent, constructing $K$ dense affinity matrices and computing SVD for each test dataset incurs an $O(K n_{T_i}^2 (d_{T_i} + d^*))$ overhead. On larger test datasets, this non-parametric graph generation step becomes a significant computational bottleneck (e.g., taking 231s out of 240s total runtime).

Writing and Presentation Quality: The manuscript exhibits numerous typos and formatting oversights throughout, such as 'Subsapmling' (Algorithm 1), 'Obatain' (Algorithm 1), 'neueral-network-computing' (p. 8), 'Multiply Band Width' (Table 7), 'time dost' (p. 19), and multiple duplicate entries in the references list (e.g., Breunig et al. 2000 cited twice on p. 10; Chen et al. 2024 on p. 10 and 11; Li et al. 2022 on p. 12; Livernoche et al. 2023 on p. 12; Ruff et al. 2018 on p. 13).

strengths: The paper addresses a challenging and practically important problem: developing a universal, zero-shot/amortized model for outlier detection (OD) on tabular datasets across diverse domains without requiring per-dataset retraining or hyperparameter tuning.

The proposed formulation circumvents feature dimensionality mismatch across heterogeneous datasets by constructing multi-bandwidth Gaussian affinity graphs and projecting them into a fixed-dimensional space via truncated SVD.
The empirical evaluation is extensive, comparing the proposed UniOD model against 15 traditional and deep learning baselines on 15 benchmark datasets from ADBench.
weaknesses: Conceptual flaw with SVD node features: SVD/spectral decomposition on adjacency matrices yields eigenvectors that suffer from sign ambiguity (arbitrary $\pm$ sign) and coordinate rotation across different graphs. Feeding raw singular vectors directly as input features to fixed-weight GIN and Graph Transformer models assumes a shared canonical coordinate alignment across disparate datasets that does not mathematically hold.

Scalability and missing implementation details: Several historical datasets used for training (e.g., http with 567k samples, cover with 286k samples, skin with 245k samples, celeba with 202k samples) are massive. Computing full $n \times n$ dense Gaussian kernels, truncated SVD, and full Graph Transformer attention ($O(n^2)$) on a single 48 GB GPU is computationally intractable without extreme subsampling or batching, yet no graph sampling or mini-batching mechanism is described in Section 3 or Algorithm 1.

Unfair supervisory advantage with marginal performance gain: UniOD is trained in a supervised manner using ground-truth anomaly labels across 15 historical datasets. In contrast, the competing baselines are entirely unsupervised. Despite this significant supervision advantage, UniOD performs on par with or worse than Isolation Forest (an unsupervised method from 2008), which achieves 45.89% AUPRC compared to UniOD's 45.43% AUPRC, and 76.62% AUROC compared to UniOD's 78.93%.

Suspicious baseline results: The KPCA+MLP baseline yields AUROCs far below 50% on several datasets (e.g., 9.8% on SpamBase, 28.7% on breastw, 39.8% on optdigits). An AUROC substantially below 50% typically indicates flipped class labels or an implementation error rather than mere poor representation learning.

Drafting and bibliography issues: Several references are duplicated verbatim in the bibliography (e.g., Breunig et al., 2000; Li et al., 2022; Ruff et al., 2018; Livernoche et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2024), along with typos in key sections (e.g., 'Subsapmling' and 'Obatain' in Algorithm 1).

strengths: The paper targets a challenging and ambitious problem: building a 'universal' zero-shot outlier detection model that transfers across heterogeneous tabular datasets with varying dimensions and domains without retraining.

The proposed formulation—converting arbitrary tabular datasets into multi-scale similarity graphs and extracting aligned representations via truncated SVD, followed by GIN and Graph Transformer architectures—is creative.
The paper provides theoretical analysis of the generalization gap across datasets using covering numbers and Rademacher complexity.
Extensive empirical comparisons are conducted on ADBench across 30+ tabular datasets and 17 baseline methods, accompanied by ablation studies.
weaknesses: Fundamental issue with spectral embeddings (sign ambiguity): UniOD constructs node features via truncated SVD on kernel matrices, $X = [u_1, \dots, u_d] \Lambda^{1/2}$. In spectral graph theory and kernel PCA, eigenvectors are uniquely defined only up to sign flips ($u_i \leftrightarrow -u_i$). The paper does not discuss or resolve eigenvector sign ambiguity, which poses a severe consistency issue when transferring a trained neural network across distinct datasets.

Marginal empirical gain over simple training-free baselines: On Group II datasets (Table 3), UniOD achieves an average AUROC of 78.52%, which is virtually indistinguishable from simple kNN (78.45%), despite kNN requiring zero historical labeled datasets, zero offline training, and significantly fewer architectural components. Given that UniOD requires labeled historical datasets and substantial model training, the modest performance advantage over kNN or ECOD weakens the practical case for the method.

Scalability bottlenecks: Generating the full similarity matrix and performing truncated SVD scales as $\mathcal{O}(n^2 d + n^2 \bar{d})$, and running Graph Transformers across all $n$ nodes scales as $\mathcal{O}(n^2)$. Due to these memory and computational constraints, the authors had to subsample larger datasets to 6,000 samples (Page 9) or chunk them into arbitrary disjoint subsets (Appendix H.10), which limits the applicability to large-scale anomaly detection settings.

Theoretical derivations appear loose: In the transition from Equation (22) to Equation (23) in Appendix A, the term $8\beta / \sqrt{n}$ abruptly appears while the Rademacher complexity in Dudley's entropy integral was integrated over sample size $M$. The interaction between the within-dataset sample size $n$ and between-dataset sample size $M$ under transductive dependence via kernel SVD requires more rigorous statistical justification.

strengths: Addresses a timely and important challenge in outlier detection (OD): developing a universal, pre-trained model capable of generalizing across tabular datasets with heterogeneous feature spaces and dimensions without dataset-specific retraining or hyperparameter tuning.

The proposed representation pipeline—constructing multi-scale Gaussian kernel similarity matrices and applying truncated SVD—is an intuitive and effective mechanism to project arbitrary feature spaces into unified, dimension-aligned graph representations.

Extensive empirical evaluation across 30 primary benchmark datasets (with cross-validation between Group I and Group II) plus 27 additional datasets from ADBench, evaluated against 17 diverse traditional, deep learning, and meta-learning baselines.

Provides a formal generalization error bound (Theorem 4.1) based on covering numbers and Rademacher complexity across multi-dataset training, supporting the empirical findings regarding the number of historical datasets and kernel bandwidths.
weaknesses: Scalability bottlenecks with dataset size ($n$): Computing $n \times n$ similarity matrices and performing SVD has $O(n^2)$ to $O(n^3)$ computational and memory complexity. Consequently, datasets larger than 6,000 samples had to be subsampled or partitioned into subsets, which significantly restricts applicability to large-scale tabular anomaly detection tasks.

Narrow performance margin over simple non-parametric baselines: On the Group II cross-validation benchmark (Table 3), UniOD achieves an average AUROC of 78.52%, which is virtually indistinguishable from standard kNN at 78.45%. On the additional 27 datasets (Table 18), UniOD (74.9%) achieves only a modest gain over kNN (74.0%). Considering the complexity of meta-training $K$ parallel GINs and Graph Transformers with labeled historical data, the practical advantage over zero-training kNN warrants deeper discussion.

Catastrophic degradation on specific datasets: On certain datasets, UniOD suffers dramatic performance drops compared to classical methods; for example, on FashionMNIST, UniOD achieves an AUROC of only 41.0% (substantially worse than random guessing), whereas kNN achieves 85.9% and IF achieves 87.7%. A discussion of when and why the universal similarity representation breaks down is missing.

Transductive constraint: Because the representation relies on the global similarity graph and SVD across the entire sample set, the framework is inherently transductive. Real-time streaming or inductive scoring of individual unseen instances requires non-trivial approximations or re-evaluating the graph, limiting online deployment scenarios.

Minor presentation issues: The abstract contains an incomplete sentence ('Our code is available at 
 1 INTRODUCTION'), and a few typos appear in the text and appendix (e.g., 'Subsapmling' in Algorithm 1, 'hyperparamter' in Section D).

strengths: Ambitious and interesting problem setting: The paper addresses the important challenge of universal outlier detection (OD) across heterogeneous tabular datasets with varying dimensionalities and domains without per-dataset retraining.

Creative unification pipeline: Using multi-scale Gaussian kernel similarity matrices followed by truncated SVD to harmonize heterogeneous feature dimensions into a standardized graph representation is an intuitive approach to dimension-agnostic tabular learning.

Extensive experimental scope: The empirical evaluation covers a large suite of benchmark datasets from ADBench (30 primary datasets plus 27 additional datasets) and compares against 17 diverse baselines spanning traditional, deep, and meta-learning OD methods.
Theoretical effort: The authors make a serious attempt to establish generalization error bounds for the multi-dataset graph-based learning framework using covering numbers and Rademacher complexity.
weaknesses: Supervised training yields marginal gains over simple unsupervised baselines: UniOD requires access to fully labeled historical datasets during training, whereas standard OD baselines (e.g., kNN, Isolation Forest, ECOD) operate purely unsupervised without any label supervision. Despite this significant supervision advantage and model complexity, UniOD's performance gain over simple classical baselines is marginal. For instance, on Group II datasets (Table 3), UniOD achieves an average AUROC of 78.52% compared to 78.45% for unsupervised kNN (a +0.07% difference). On the 27 additional ADBench datasets (Table 18), UniOD achieves 74.9% vs. 74.0% for kNN.

Severe scalability bottlenecks due to quadratic space and time complexity: Constructing dense $n \times n$ similarity matrices, computing truncated SVDs, and running Graph Transformers / dense GIN message passing require $O(n^2)$ memory and computation. Consequently, the method cannot directly handle datasets with large sample sizes. The authors are forced to cap datasets at 6,000 samples or partition them into disjoint subsets (Section H.10). In outlier detection, subsampling and chunking alter local density and neighborhood structures, severely limiting the framework's applicability to large tabular datasets.

Questionable assumptions and vacuity in the theoretical analysis: Theorem 4.1 assumes that the historical datasets $\mathcal{D}_H$ are sampled i.i.d. from a meta-distribution over datasets. In practice, tabular datasets from diverse real-world domains have vastly different generative processes, feature types, and anomaly definitions, violating the i.i.d. assumption. Furthermore, with $M = 15$ historical datasets and constants that grow exponentially with network depth ($b_W^{L L'}$), the generalization bound is practically vacuous.

Lack of essential architectural ablations: The model architecture is complex, combining $K$ parallel GINs, $K$ parallel Graph Transformers, and an MLP head. However, the ablation study (Section 5.3) only investigates the number of historical datasets $M$ and bandwidths $K$. There is no ablation evaluating GIN alone versus Graph Transformer alone, leaving it unclear whether both components are necessary or which provides the actual inductive bias.

Severe performance degradation on multiple benchmark datasets: UniOD exhibits dramatic collapse on several datasets in Table 18. For instance, on FashionMNIST, UniOD achieves an AUROC of 41.0% (substantially worse than random guessing), whereas kNN achieves 85.9% and ECOD achieves 87.8%. Similarly poor performance occurs on annthyroid (68.8% vs. 81.5% for IF) and vertebral (28.6% vs. 36.8% for IF). The manuscript does not offer an adequate analysis of why the universal representation fails so drastically on these tasks.
